title: Java Collections
objectives: Choose the right collection for a workload

sections.markdown: The Collections Framework is a unified set of interfaces (List, Set, Map, Queue) and implementations for storing and manipulating groups of objects.

sections.code:
HashMap internals:
  bucket = hash(key) & (capacity-1)
  collisions -> linked list, then a balanced TREE if a bucket > 8 (Java 8+)
  load factor 0.75 -> resize (double) & rehash

sections.markdown: Java 8 upgraded HashMap buckets from linked lists to **red-black trees** once a bucket exceeds 8 entries, improving worst-case from O(n) to O(log n).
Using a key whose hashCode/equals you didn't override (or that's mutable) — lookups silently fail. Map keys should be immutable with correct equals/hashCode.
Default to ArrayList and HashMap. Use ConcurrentHashMap (not Hashtable) for concurrency; use the right Set/Map when you need ordering or sorting.

flashcards.back: ArrayList: O(1) index, cache-friendly. LinkedList: O(1) insert/remove at ends, O(n) access.

flashcards.front: How does HashMap handle collisions in Java 8+?
flashcards.back: Chaining; a bucket converts to a red-black tree past 8 entries for O(log n) worst case.
HashMap: O(1), unordered. TreeMap: O(log n), sorted by key.

quiz.q: Which gives O(1) average lookup AND sorted keys?
options: Neither — you trade one for the other
quiz.explain: HashMap is O(1) unordered; TreeMap is sorted but O(log n). You can't have both.

quiz.q: Java 8 HashMap buckets become trees after about…
quiz.explain: Treeification kicks in past 8 entries in a bucket.
ConcurrentHashMap offers fine-grained concurrency without locking the whole map.

challenges.text: Count word frequencies in a text using a HashMap.
Implement an LRU cache using LinkedHashMap's accessOrder.
Build a custom key class with correct equals/hashCode and verify map behavior.
Benchmark ArrayList vs LinkedList vs ArrayDeque for queue operations.
